newsitem.title: USA: U.S. opposes taking elephants from endangered list.
newsitem.headline: U.S. opposes taking elephants from endangered list.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it would oppose a move by Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe to take their elephant populations off the endangered list.
The action would occur at a meeting this month of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in Harare, Zimbabwe.
"The administration remains firmly opposed to any resumption of trade in ivory," said Donald Barry, acting assistant secretary for fish and wildlife and parks.
While the United States recognised the successful efforts of the three countries to manage their herds, Barry said easing trade restrictions would pose "unacceptable risks to elephant populations."

"We have yet to have an airtight system that has precluded illegal ivory from getting to markets like Japan," he said, citing a report by a unit of the World Wildlife Fund that found trade in illegal ivory was active in Asia.
Environmental groups were split over the request by Botswana, Namibia, and Zimbabwe. They predicted the U.S. position would trigger a fight at the CITES meeting in Harare, which begins on June 9.
"This will probably be the most contentious issue, especially since Zimbabwe is the host," said Wayne Pacelle, vice president of the Humane Society of the United States.
Officials from African elephant range countries were set to meet in Harare on Wednesday to decide their position on the proposal by the three southern African nations.
"We believe we satisfy the criteria for downlisting," said Mustaq Moorad, counsellor at the Botswana Embassy in Washington, adding the CITES panel of experts recently endorsed that view.

The three countries need support from two-thirds of the CITES members to get their elephant populations off the endangered list, which they have tried to do at the last three CITES meetings since 1990.

Moorad said it was unclear whether they would be able to secure enough votes now that the United States has said it would oppose them. "That's our dilemma now, because the U.S. is a major voice at every international forum."
The elephant population in Botswana is now too large to sustain, he said, with the animals crowding people off land and trampling crops in the northwestern part of the country.
